strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and practically relevant problem: making human activity recognition from motion time series more flexible, interpretable, and less dependent on task-specific classifier heads.

The proposed system combines several sensible components: pairwise feature-importance knowledge, class-wise retrieval over sensor embeddings, reciprocal-rank fusion across placements, and staged LLM prompting. The overall pipeline is clearly motivated and mostly understandable.

Empirical coverage is broad for HAR: eight public datasets with varied class counts, sensors, placements, and difficulty levels. The reported gains over direct LLM prompting and cross-modal zero-shot baselines are large.

The ablations are useful. Removing retrieval, pruning, or prior feature knowledge all causes substantial drops, which supports the claim that the method’s performance is not simply due to the base LLM.
The appendix includes baseline details, dataset splits, prompt templates, feature definitions, per-class results, and retrieval latency, which improves transparency relative to many LLM-agent papers.
weaknesses: The central “zero-shot” and “classifier-free generalization” claims are overstated. ZARA builds a labeled retrieval database and an activity-pair feature-importance knowledge base from the same activity labels used at inference. This is not zero-shot recognition of unseen classes in the usual sense; it is closer to supervised nonparametric classification with an LLM reasoning layer and held-out subjects.

The comparison to many baselines is not fully fair. Several baselines are evaluated as true zero-shot models without access to the same labeled database, feature statistics, or pairwise class knowledge that ZARA uses. The strongest supervised embedding baselines in Table 2 are a more appropriate comparison, and ZARA is competitive but not uniformly better than Mantis with a trained head.

The experimental protocol uses small randomly sampled inference subsets because of API cost, but the paper reports no confidence intervals, repeated sampling, statistical tests, or sensitivity to random seeds. This weakens confidence in the large claimed gains, especially on datasets with only 10 to 50 windows per class.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank in the manuscript, and the main model relies on Gemini-2.0-Flash, a proprietary API whose behavior, availability, and versioning may change. Temperature 0 alone does not make the full pipeline reproducible.

The paper does not convincingly evaluate the faithfulness or utility of the generated explanations. The rationales are generated from selected features and retrieved class statistics, but there is no human evaluation, causal faithfulness test, or error analysis showing that the explanations are reliable rather than plausible post-hoc narratives.

There are unresolved leakage and scope concerns. Mantis is acknowledged to have been pretrained on HAR datasets including UCI-HAR, and the paper notes possible baseline pretraining overlap but does not systematically control for it. The knowledge base also appears activity-set-specific, despite claims of label-inventory agnosticism.

The contribution’s relevance to ACL/NLP is somewhat indirect. The LLM prompting and rationale generation are NLP-relevant, but the main technical substance and evaluation are primarily in wearable sensing/HAR rather than language processing, and the paper does not deeply study language-model behavior beyond using agents as decision modules.

Writing and presentation need polishing: there are typos, missing code URL, inconsistent terminology around zero-shot/open-set/subject-holdout, and some claims such as “ready for real-world use” are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting problem: making HAR from motion time series more flexible and interpretable by combining retrieval, handcrafted feature statistics, and LLM-based reasoning.

The system is described at a reasonably concrete level, including the pairwise feature knowledge base, class-wise retrieval, pruning, and final decision stages, and the appendix includes prompt templates and dataset preprocessing details.

The empirical coverage is broad, with eight public HAR datasets, multiple sensor configurations, several baseline families, and ablations for retrieval, pruning, prior knowledge, and retrieval encoder choice.
The ablation results are directionally useful: retrieval, feature knowledge, and candidate pruning each appear to contribute substantially to the reported performance.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot/classifier-free claim is not well supported. ZARA builds a labeled vector database and a pairwise feature-importance knowledge base from the same dataset label inventory, apparently including all candidate activities. This is closer to supervised retrieval/prototype-based recognition on held-out subjects than true zero-shot recognition of unseen classes or new sensor setups.

The comparison to baselines appears unfair or at least insufficiently controlled. ZARA uses labeled per-class examples and supervised feature-importance estimates, while several baselines are evaluated as generic zero-shot models without comparable access to labeled support data, class-wise retrieval statistics, or engineered feature distributions.

The methodology relies on supervised offline components despite emphasizing no task-specific classifiers. The AutoGluon permutation feature ranking over activity pairs, labeled retrieval database, and class-wise statistics are substantial task-specific adaptation; the distinction from training a classifier is therefore overstated.

The experimental protocol evaluates held-out subjects, not genuinely unseen activities. Claims about plug-and-play generalization to new activities and label-inventory agnosticism are not validated by leave-class-out, cross-dataset, new-sensor-placement, or new-label experiments.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank, inference uses proprietary Gemini/GPT models, exact sampled evaluation instances and seeds are not specified, and only small balanced subsets are evaluated because of API cost.

The reported gains are very large but lack uncertainty estimates, repeated sampling, statistical tests, or sensitivity analysis for prompt wording, retrieved top-k, number of selected features, and LLM stochastic/API/version variation.

The interpretability claim is under-evaluated. The paper provides generated rationales, but does not test whether they are faithful to the actual decision process, robust to perturbations, or useful to humans beyond being plausible natural-language explanations.

The paper is only partially aligned with ACL/NLP expectations. The NLP contribution is mostly using an off-the-shelf LLM as a controller over engineered time-series features; the main technical contribution lies in HAR retrieval and feature engineering rather than language modeling or linguistic analysis.

Presentation contains overclaiming and some polish issues, including repeated assertions of SOTA zero-shot performance despite the supervised support database, and minor writing/formatting problems such as missing code URL and grammatical errors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: flexible human activity recognition from motion time series without training a task-specific classifier at inference time, with natural-language rationales.

ZARA is a coherent system combining interpretable handcrafted features, pairwise feature-importance knowledge, class-wise retrieval, and staged LLM reasoning. The components are well motivated and the overall pipeline is clearly explained.

Empirical coverage is broad for HAR: 8 public datasets with varying numbers of classes, sensor placements, and difficulty levels, plus comparisons against LLM prompting, multimodal contrastive models, and time-series foundation encoders.
The reported gains over classifier-free baselines are large, and the ablations support the importance of retrieval, pruning, and prior feature knowledge.
The appendix improves reproducibility by listing datasets, preprocessing choices, baseline adaptations, feature groups, latency measurements, per-class results, and prompt templates.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot claim is overstated. ZARA requires a labeled retrieval database containing the candidate activity classes and constructs pairwise feature-importance knowledge from labeled data. This is closer to classifier-free supervised retrieval/adaptation than true zero-shot recognition of unseen activities.

The paper repeatedly claims plug-and-play generalization, but adding a new activity still requires labeled windows to update feature statistics and retrieval evidence. This weakens the main conceptual contribution and should be framed more precisely.

Evaluation uses small randomly sampled inference subsets due to API cost, sometimes only 10-50 windows per class. The paper does not provide enough information about random seeds, variance, confidence intervals, or robustness across multiple samples, so the reliability of the large reported gains is hard to assess.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. Some baselines are constrained by input format or single-sensor assumptions, while ZARA uses labeled class-wise retrieval and handcrafted feature distributions from the same benchmark domain. The comparison to true zero-shot multimodal models may therefore exaggerate the advantage.

The method depends heavily on proprietary or API-based LLM behavior, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze sensitivity to LLM choice, prompt variation, parsing failures, cost, or reproducibility of model outputs beyond using temperature 0.

The explanations are claimed to be verifiable, but the evaluation focuses on classification accuracy. There is no systematic assessment of rationale faithfulness, calibration, or whether cited features genuinely caused the decisions.
The abstract states that code is available but the URL appears blank in the manuscript, which is a concrete reproducibility issue.

The contribution is relevant and promising, but because the main claim is somewhat mischaracterized and the empirical protocol has notable reproducibility and statistical limitations, I view it as borderline for Findings rather than a clear acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles a clear and relevant problem for LLM-based time-series reasoning: direct prompting over raw sensor streams is poorly grounded, while conventional HAR models require task-specific training. The proposed separation between statistical motion priors and local retrieved evidence is well motivated.

ZARA is methodologically coherent: pairwise feature-importance profiling, placement-specific retrieval, class-wise multi-sensor fusion, candidate pruning, and final LLM reasoning form a plausible pipeline for interpretable, training-free inference at test time.

The empirical evaluation is broad in dataset coverage, spanning eight HAR benchmarks and both cross-subject and cross-dataset settings. The reported gains over raw LLM prompting, multimodal prompting, and several pretrained HAR/embedding baselines are large.

The ablations are useful and support the central design choices: removing retrieval, pruning, or prior-knowledge injection substantially reduces performance, suggesting that improvements do not come solely from the LLM backbone.

The appendix provides many implementation details, including dataset preprocessing, baseline adaptations, retrieval backbones, token usage, feature definitions, and prompt templates, which improves reproducibility relative to many LLM-agent papers.
weaknesses: The term “training-free” is somewhat overstated. ZARA avoids neural parameter updates at inference, but it still requires labeled support data, class labels for class-conditional retrieval, and offline AutoGluon/permutation-based pairwise feature profiling. This is closer to labeled-support-set reasoning than true zero-shot or calibration-free deployment.

The cross-dataset setting is limited by the fact that retrieval evidence is still built from the target dataset. Thus the experiment mainly tests transfer of feature-selection priors, not full cross-domain deployment without labeled target-domain data. The paper should state this limitation more prominently and temper claims about plug-and-play generalization.

Evaluation subsets are small and randomly sampled, apparently for API-cost reasons, with no confidence intervals, repeated sampling runs, or statistical significance tests. This weakens confidence in the magnitude and stability of the reported gains, especially on datasets with many classes and only 10-20 windows per class.

Several baselines seem disadvantaged or not directly comparable. Raw LLM prompting baselines are expected to perform poorly, while stronger non-LLM HAR baselines with full supervised training are not included as context. For pretrained methods, details on label text prompts, sensor handling, and whether best-of-sensor selection gives comparable access to multi-sensor information need clearer justification.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the abstract says code is available but the URL is blank, and the main results depend on proprietary or evolving LLMs such as Gemini-2.0-Flash and GPT-4.1-mini. Temperature 0 alone does not guarantee exact reproducibility across API versions.

The method’s cost and scalability are only partially addressed. Token usage is reported, but end-to-end latency and monetary cost of the multi-agent LLM pipeline are not compared against simpler kNN/prototype/statistical classifiers that use the same engineered features and labeled support set.

The contribution is somewhat peripheral to core NLP: the main technical object is an HAR time-series classification system, with LLMs used as reasoning controllers over engineered tables. The NLP relevance is present through language-based reasoning and RAG, but the paper should better articulate what general lesson it contributes to computational linguistics beyond this application domain.

The generated rationales are claimed to improve trust, but they are not evaluated for faithfulness beyond task accuracy. Since the LLM reasons over selected summaries rather than the raw signal, rationale validity should be tested or the interpretability claim should be softened.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored interface between LLM/RAG methods and wearable-sensor activity recognition, with a clear motivation: raw time-series are hard for LLMs to interpret without structured grounding.

The proposed system is reasonably well articulated at a high level: statistical feature profiling, class-wise retrieval, rank fusion, feature selection, pruning, and final decision agents are described coherently.
The empirical section is broad in surface coverage, spanning eight HAR datasets, several LLM backbones, cross-subject and cross-dataset-style settings, and multiple ablations.

The appendix includes useful details such as baseline descriptions, dataset splits, token usage, per-class results, retrieval latency, feature categories, and prompt templates, which improves transparency relative to many LLM-agent papers.
The ablations consistently suggest that retrieval, pruning, and prior feature knowledge each contribute to the reported performance.
weaknesses: The central framing as “training-free,” “zero-training,” and “open-set” is misleading. ZARA relies heavily on labeled support data, pairwise activity feature-importance estimation using AutoGluon, class-conditional retrieval, and target-domain labeled databases. Avoiding neural parameter updates is not the same as avoiding supervised adaptation.

The experimental comparison is not fully fair. ZARA uses labeled database information and statistically optimized handcrafted features, while many main baselines are evaluated as zero-shot or frozen models without an equivalent labeled-support feature/classification pipeline. A simple kNN, nearest-centroid, random forest/SVM, AutoGluon, or calibrated feature-table classifier using the same extracted features and support data is essential but missing.

The cross-dataset claims are overstated. In the “cross-dataset” setting, retrieval evidence is still built from the target dataset; only the feature-prior knowledge is transferred. This substantially weakens the claim of robust cross-domain generalization across heterogeneous sensor domains.

Evaluation uses small randomly sampled inference subsets, often only 190-288 windows per dataset, despite much larger available test sets. The paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance, making the large claimed gains hard to trust.

There is potential methodological circularity in using supervised pairwise feature-importance profiles as “knowledge” and then crediting the LLM agent for discriminative reasoning. Much of the predictive signal may come from the supervised profiling and class-wise statistics rather than from language-model reasoning.

The paper does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of the LLM. Deterministic non-LLM decision rules over the same selected features and retrieved class distributions would be a necessary control.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the appendix. The abstract’s code link appears blank, exact sampling indices and random seeds are not provided, AutoGluon settings and feature extraction details are underspecified, and several results depend on proprietary or changing LLM APIs.

The baseline treatment raises concerns. Some baselines are constrained by input format or single-sensor assumptions, while ZARA is allowed multi-sensor class-wise retrieval and labeled support statistics. This may exaggerate the apparent superiority of the proposed method.

The manuscript’s relevance to ACL/NLP is somewhat marginal. The primary contribution is a supervised sensor-classification pipeline with LLM prompting as a decision layer; the linguistic or NLP methodological contribution is limited.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, including “state-of-the-art,” “plug-and-play,” “open-set,” “trustworthy,” and “verifiable.” The generated rationales may be plausible explanations of feature comparisons, but the paper does not evaluate rationale faithfulness or user-facing interpretability.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful reframing of LLM-based HAR: instead of asking an LLM to directly interpret raw sensor streams, it builds statistically grounded textual priors and retrieves local evidence for grounded reasoning. This is a compelling direction for making LLM use in time-series settings less ad hoc.

The empirical results are strong across eight HAR benchmarks, with large gains over direct text/table/plot prompting and several pretrained motion/time-series baselines in the reported parameter-frozen setting. The paper also evaluates multiple LLM backbones, which helps show that the gains are not tied to a single proprietary model.

The method is reasonably interpretable: the pairwise feature-importance knowledge base, class-wise retrieval, pruning stage, and final rationale all expose intermediate evidence rather than producing only a label.

The ablation studies are useful and support the central design choices. Removing retrieval, evidence pruning, or prior knowledge all causes substantial drops, which strengthens the case that ZARA’s performance is not merely due to a strong base LLM.
The appendix provides helpful implementation detail, including dataset splits, preprocessing, retrieval backbones, token usage, per-class results, and prompt templates.
weaknesses: The “training-free” framing is somewhat overstated. ZARA does not update neural weights, but it relies on labeled support data, class-wise retrieval databases, and AutoGluon-based pairwise feature profiling. This is closer to non-parametric supervised adaptation than genuinely training-free recognition, and the paper should be more precise about this distinction.

The fairness of the main comparison is not fully convincing. Many main baselines are direct zero-shot or classifier-free methods, while ZARA uses labeled in-domain support data to build both evidence and statistical priors. The supervised-head comparisons in Table 2 are helpful, but the main claims would be stronger with more direct comparisons to kNN, classical feature-based classifiers, and lightweight supervised baselines under matched support-data access.

The cross-dataset evaluation still appears to use labeled target-domain retrieval databases, transferring only the knowledge component. This limits the strength of the claim about cross-dataset generalization, since the method is not operating in a target-label-free transfer setting.

Evaluation is based on relatively small randomly sampled inference subsets because of API cost, with no apparent confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple random seeds. Given the small per-class sample sizes on several datasets, the magnitude and stability of the reported gains are harder to assess.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract has an empty code link, proprietary LLMs are central to the strongest results, and important stochastic choices such as sampling seeds are not clearly specified. Temperature 0 helps, but API model drift and unavailable code would still make exact reproduction difficult.

Computational and practical cost is only partially addressed. Token usage and retrieval latency are reported, but the full cost of multi-agent LLM inference, AutoGluon profiling over all activity pairs, and scaling to larger activity libraries is not thoroughly analyzed.

The relevance to ACL/NLP is present through LLM/RAG/agentic reasoning, but the main task and evaluation are primarily wearable-sensor HAR. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what general NLP or language-based reasoning insight is learned beyond this application domain.
